Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
 CORE
January 30, 2025
Matthew S. Austin, MD
Noam Shohat, MD
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the various types of instability after total knee arthroplasty and their causes.
Recognize the symptoms and clinical findings associated with instability after total knee
arthroplasty.
Understand the diagnostic workup for suspected instability after total knee arthroplasty.
Discuss the role of various treatment modalities for each type of instability after total knee
arthroplasty.
Introduction
Instability is a common cause of failed total knee arthroplasty (TKA).
The goal is to prevent instability via sound surgical technique.
Other reasons for failure must be excluded.




NOTES

The type and etiology of the instability pattern should be determined if possible.
Simple treatment solutions that do not correct the underlying pathology should be avoided.

Introduction
Knee instability is one of the most common causes of patient dissatisfaction and implant
failure after TKA, necessitating revision surgery.1 Instability may present early
(immediately postoperatively) because of gap or coronal imbalance, poor design, and/or
component malpositioning. Instability also may develop over time because of
polyethylene wear, aseptic loosening, and ligamentous failure. Infection always is a
concern because it may be misidentified by the patient as instability. A definitive
diagnosis may be challenging. A thorough diagnostic workup must be performed if
instability is suspected, and the type of instability must be determined. Objective
physical examination findings to support instability must be documented. A treatment
strategy, initially focused on nonsurgical management, should be developed based on
the severity of symptoms. If considering revision surgery, surgeons should remember
that the simplest options may leave the underlying cause unaddressed and may be
insufficient to improve patient outcomes. Finally, the avoidance of pitfalls that result in
instability remains an effective strategy to avoid instability after TKA, and all efforts
should be focused on attaining a stable knee during index TKA. Several subtypes of knee
instability exist; however, this lesson reviews extension, flexion, and mid-flexion
instability. Patellofemoral, genu recurvatum, and global instability are beyond the scope
of this lesson.
Incidence
Instability is a common cause of failed TKA.
Accounts for 10% to 25% of all revision TKA procedures

Incidence
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
2/22

Instability is the third most common cause of failure after TKA and is responsible for 10%
to 25% of all revision procedures and almost 40% of early revision procedures.1
Instability also has been suggested as a major contributing factor to the relatively high
dissatisfaction rate (approximately 20%) in patients who undergo TKA.
Types
Instability can occur early (immediately postoperatively) or late.
Instability can be crudely categorized into the following types:
Extension instability
Flexion instability
Mid-flexion instability
Patellofemoral instability, recurvatum, and multidirectional instability (not discussed in this
lesson)

Types
Extension instability may be symmetric, from excessive distal femur removal or
asymmetric because of insufficient or excessive soft-tissue release.
Flexion instability may result from distinct factors, including posterior offset restoration,
malrotation of the femoral component, or an excessive tibial slope.
Late instability may result from polyethylene wear, component loosening, tibial post
fracture in the posterior-stabilized implants (Figure 1), and posterior cruciate ligament
(PCL) insufficiency in cruciate-retaining implants (flexion type).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
3/22

Figure 1 Clinical photograph shows a fracture of the tibial post in a posterior-stabilized
total knee arthroplasty implant, which led to instability. (Courtesy of Matthew S. Austin,
MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
Evaluation and Diagnosis

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Symptomatic instability after TKA can be described as imbalance and excessive
movement in one or more planes of the artificial joint that is associated with a
supporting clinical presentation. Instability may be present in patients without
symptoms or dissatisfaction. Therefore, an extensive workup must be performed before
determining that instability is the cause necessitating revision.
Patient History
The patient history should focus on the following:
Indication for index TKA and associated comorbidities (connective tissue disease,
inflammatory or Charcot arthropathy)
Previous deformity or surgical procedures on the knee
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
4/22

Timing of onset of symptoms
Presence and location of pain

Patient History
The patient history should focus on the reason for index TKA, the degree of coronal
deformity, previous surgical procedures on the joint, preoperative range of motion
(ROM; including the presence of recurvatum), and the type of prosthesis used.
Numerous comorbidities have been suggested as risk factors for instability, including
rheumatoid arthritis, connective tissue diseases, severe osteoporosis, obesity, and
neuropathy (Charcot joint). A more severe preoperative angular deformity is more
difficult to balance and predisposes patients to postoperative instability. The onset of
instability is important for the diagnosis because it aids in understanding the underlying
mechanism of the instability and possible treatment options. Early instability usually
results from suboptimal intraoperative soft-tissue balancing, whereas new instability in a
previously well-functioning joint may suggest loosening, wear, or ligament insufficiency.
Symptoms
Symptoms range from subtle discomfort to gross dislocation.
A sensation of the knee giving way is common.
Pain may or may not be present.

Symptoms
Instability can present in various manners, ranging from subtle discomfort and distrust
of the knee to gross dislocation. A common report is of the knee giving way or buckling,
especially when ascending and descending stairs or rising from a sitting
position. Abnormal gait (thrust) and stiffness and pain and guarding are other symptoms
associated with ligament insufficiency. Anterior knee pain and recurrent joint effusions
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
5/22

secondary to anterior tibial translation also may occur. The patient should be queried
about his or her impression of the direction of the instability.
Physical Examination
Observe for gait abnormalities, especially signs of thrust.
Palpate muscles and examine ROM.
Assess stability in the coronal and sagittal planes at 0°, 30°, and 90°.

Physical Examination
Gait mechanics should be observed. A varus thrust indicates lateral instability, whereas a
valgus thrust (less common) suggests medial instability (Video 1). Muscle strength must
be examined because weakness may produce symptoms similar to those of instability.
Recurrent effusions also are common. Palpation of muscle insertion points may reveal
tenderness. ROM must be assessed because a residual flexion contracture limiting full
extension may result in early fatigue and a sensation of giving way without true
instability. The mediolateral opening should be assessed in full extension, in 90° of
flexion, and within that range (usually 30° of flexion) to define the type of instability.
Anteroposterior instability can be assessed via the anterior and posterior drawer tests
with the knee at 90° and the leg completely relaxed. Some surgeons find it helpful to
perform anteroposterior testing with the patient seated on the edge of the examination
table and the knee flexed to 90°, with the weight of the foot fully supported. Tibial
translation commonly is measured and graded into one of the following categories: less
than 5 mm, 5 to 10 mm, or more than 10 mm. Guarding because of pain may obscure
substantial instability. Prosthesis design also affects these measurements and should be
noted.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
6/22

Video 1 Austin MS: Video. Varus Thrust Gait. Philadelphia, PA, 2021.
Imaging Studies
Standard radiographs include standing full-length AP, lateral, and skyline views (Figure 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
7/22

Figure 2 AP (A), lateral (B), and skyline (C) radiographs demonstrate a knee dislocation after
total knee arthroplasty. (Courtesy of Matthew S. Austin, MD, Philadelphia, PA.
Optional radiographs include AP and mediolateral stress views.
CT scans may provide information on component rotation.

Imaging Studies
Radiographs are inexpensive and readily available and may provide valuable information
on the cause of instability. Standing full-length AP radiographs may provide information
on overall mechanical alignment, joint line obliquity, and the lateral distal femur and
medial proximal tibia angles. Lateral radiographs allow for assessment of tibial slope,
joint height, and component sizing. AP instability also can be evaluated on lateral
radiographs by assessing tibial translation between full extension and full flexion. Skyline
radiographs facilitate evaluation of the location of the patella in the femoral groove,
patellar subluxation, and the status of the patellar component.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
8/22

Classic radiographic findings include a distalized femoral component, lack of posterior
offset restoration, and excessive tibial resection. Current radiographs always should be
compared with preoperative and immediate postoperative radiographs, especially in
patients with late instability. Stress radiographs evaluate the degree of ligament laxity or
insufficiency and may provide additional information. Fluoroscopic examination may be
useful in select patients to objectively demonstrate abnormal kinematics. CT may be
performed if malrotation is suspected.
Laboratory Studies
Infection should be ruled out in every patient in whom instability is suspected.
Serum tests should include C-reactive protein levels and erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
If serum markers are elevated or high and clinical suspicion for infection exists, then joint
aspiration should be performed.

Laboratory Studies
Infection must be ruled out during the evaluation of a painful knee, especially if revision
surgery is planned. Recent guidelines support laboratory screening via C-reactive protein
levels and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. If either of these markers is elevated or
clinical suspicion for infection exists—because of erythema, redness, fever, a history of
infection, or delayed wound healing— joint aspiration should be performed and the fluid
should be sent for culture, sensitivities, synovial white blood cell count, and
polymorphonuclear percentage.
Extension Instability
Types
Extension instability may be symmetric or asymmetric.
The type of instability must be determined because management differs between the two
types.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
9/22


Types
Extension instability commonly is divided into two different entities: symmetric and
asymmetric. Symmetric types result from inappropriate bone resection, whereas
asymmetric types result from inappropriate soft-tissue tension.
Symmetric Type
In this type of instability, a rectangular extension gap is adequately achieved; however,
mediolateral instability is present and may result from one of the following factors:
Excessive distal femur resection, resulting in joint line elevation and flexion-extension
mismatch
Excessive proximal tibia resection, usually resulting in instability in flexion and extension
Asymmetric Type
Asymmetric instability is more commonly encountered than symmetric instability. In
asymmetric instability, a rectangular extension gap is not achieved, and it remains trapezoidal
after soft-tissue release and bone cuts. This type of instability may result from one of the
following factors:
Incomplete soft-tissue release of the concave side of the deformity, resulting in under-
correction of the angular deformity
Overcorrection or complete rupture of the collateral ligaments on the concave side of the
angular deformity
In patients with severe deformity, attenuation of the collateral ligaments on the convex side
of the deformity may be present.
Findings

Findings
Extension instability is easily diagnosed if the knee is unstable to mediolateral
(varus/valgus) stress in extension. Inadequate release or insufficiency of an isolated
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
10/22

collateral ligament can be diagnosed if only one side (medial or lateral) opens in
extension.
Management
The best treatment option for instability is prevention; however, management differ between
the two types of extension instability.
Symmetric Type
Preventive measures are used to avoid over-resection of the distal femur.
If too much distal femur has been resected, augments are used.
If too much proximal tibia has been resected, polyethylene thickness is upsized.

Symmetric Type
Symmetric instability can be avoided by cutting the distal femur appropriately. A
widespread practice is to elevate the joint line in patients with flexion contraction to
overcome the overtightened posterior capsule and gain full extension. Therefore, proper
posterior soft-tissue release and osteophyte removal generally should be performed
before cutting an additional amount from the distal femur.
If too much bone has been resected from the proximal tibia, exchange of the
polyethylene component for a thicker component is appropriate;2 however, if instability
is isolated to extension only because of excessive distal femur removal and joint line
elevation, changing to a thicker polyethylene liner may result in a flexion gap that is too
tight. In such patients, augmentation of the distal femur should be considered to restore
the joint line and avoid flexion tightness.
Asymmetric Type
Preventive measures are used to avoid insufficient or excessive soft-tissue releases.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
11/22

Acute ligamentous transection can be managed via primary repair.
If the collateral ligaments are insufficient, a constrained prosthesis is used.

Asymmetric Type
To avoid asymmetric gap formation, mediolateral stability must be achieved via
adequate soft-tissue release. A stepwise, gradual sequence of release on the concave
side should be performed based on the severity of the angular deformity.
Preoperatively, a proper evaluation of the knee should be performed, including an
evaluation of mediolateral stability to assess for collateral ligament attenuation. In
patients in whom a definite end point cannot be determined, a high index of suspicion
for ligamentous insufficiency should be maintained, and a constrained prosthesis should
be available.
If the collateral ligament is noted to be insufficient intraoperatively, hindering proper
balance, a constrained prosthesis should be considered. The amount of constraint
should be selected based on the severity of the instability. If overly aggressive soft-tissue
release or complete transection has occurred, acute collateral ligament repair with the
use of sutures or anchors can be performed, followed by the use of a hinged knee brace
for 6 weeks postoperatively.3 The repair should be assessed intraoperatively; if the knee
remains unstable, the degree of constraint should be increased in a stepwise fashion
until stability is achieved.
Flexion Instability
Definition and Causes
Laxity in the anterior-posterior plane with the knee flexed
Results from a flexion gap larger than the extension gap
Early instability may be evident shortly after surgical management. Causes include an
undersized femoral component (from over-resection of the posterior condyles), an insufficient
distal femur cut (an undersized polyethylene liner to compensate for a tight extension gap), a
steep tibial slope, and a deficient PCL with the use of a cruciate-retaining implant. Inserting the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
12/22

femoral component in excessive internal or external rotation may cause not only
patellofemoral tracking problems but also a trapezoidal flexion gap, resulting in asymmetric
flexion instability.
Late instability may result from posteromedial polyethylene wear in any TKA implant. In
cruciate-retaining implants, PCL attenuation or rupture may be an etiology. Attenuation of the
posterior capsule also may contribute to the gradual development of flexion instability.

Definition and Causes
Flexion instability may present as an isolated entity or occur in combination with
instability in other planes. As an isolated entity, flexion instability results from a flexion
gap larger than the extension gap. Several factors may lead to flexion instability.
Findings

Findings
In patients in whom TKA fails, diagnosis of instability as the cause of symptoms is difficult
because many patients with laxity in flexion are asymptomatic. Therefore, the diagnosis
should be based on a combination of patient symptoms and clinical findings to support
the symptoms. Flexion instability is assessed via the anterior and posterior drawer tests
with the knee at 90° of flexion. A modification of the quadriceps active test with the
patient in a sitting position also has been described. In general, translation greater than
1 cm is considered excessive (Video 2). Often, a posterior sag also may be observed with
PCL deficiency in a cruciate-retaining implant or a broken post in a posterior-stabilized
implant. Recurrent effusions and diffuse tenderness over the ligamentous insertion
points (mainly the pes anserinus and hamstring) also have been described. With time, a
flexion contraction may develop secondary to a fatigued extensor mechanism. Instability
in more than one plane can be assessed by examining the mediolateral opening with the
knee in 90°.Such instability may indicate that the femoral component has been
malrotated. CT can help to objectively define this parameter.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
13/22

Video 2 Austin MS: Video. Anterior/Posterior Drawer Test Assessing Flexion Instability at 90°.
Philadelphia, PA, 2021.
Imaging Studies
Normal radiographs do not exclude instability.

Imaging Studies
Flexion instability often is present in patients with normal radiographs. Several findings
are associated with flexion instability, including distalization of the joint line (more than 6
mm) on full-length AP radiographs, decreased posterior condylar offset (less than 4 mm),
increased anterior or posterior tibial translation, and a steep tibial slope on weight-
bearing lateral radiographs.
Management
Surgical management should be tailored to the specific etiology.
A small femoral component can be revised to a larger component with posterior augments.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
14/22

A steep slope can be decreased.
A failed PCL in a cruciate-retaining knee can be managed via exchange to a prosthesis (anterior
lipped polyethylene) or conversion to a posterior-stabilized implant.
If mediolateral instability also is present, a constrained component should be considered.
Constraint should be considered in a stepwise fashion, using appropriate designs to achieve
stability while avoiding overly zealous use of constrained components.

Management
Similar to extension instability, prevention of early flexion instability during index TKA is
paramount. Care should be taken to avoid over-resecting the posterior condyles and
cutting the tibia with excessive slope. Careful assessment of knee kinematics and PCL
function will facilitate selection of the correct type of prosthesis and constraint and
correct rotational alignment of the femoral prosthesis.
Flexion instability can be managed via revision surgery; however, in subtle cases,
nonsurgical management may play a role. Quadriceps fatigue secondary to the need to
relocate the tibia before proper extension can be managed via physical therapy and
strengthening. A knee brace also may play a role in management before revision
surgery.
Revision surgery should include correction of the mechanical issues leading to the
increased flexion gap. A complete physical examination should be performed under
anesthesia (Videos 3 and 4). The surgeon must evaluate flexion and extension gaps and
the tibial slope and joint line intraoperatively before deciding on the final treatment
option. The following sequence of assessment and correction can be followed to
systematically manage the common causes of flexion instability: tibial slope, component
rotation, and upsizing. Gaps should be reassessed after correction.4
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
15/22

Video 3 Austin MS: Video. Evaluation Under Anesthesia Demonstrating Flexion Instability.
Philadelphia, PA, 2021.
Video 4 Austin MS: Video. Intraoperative Evaluation of Knee Stability. Philadelphia, PA,
2021.
In patients with excessive tibial slope, the tibial component must be removed. After
recutting the proximal tibia and correcting the slope, flexion and extension gaps and the
joint line should be re-evaluated. If flexion instability remains; a larger femoralSEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
16/22

prosthesis should be considered. If flexion and extension are increased, the joint line
determines whether an increase in polyethylene component size or distalization of the
femoral component with augments is necessary.
If the slope appears correct, the size of the femoral component can be increased with or
without the addition of augments; upsizing the femur often leads to a gap between the
posterior condyle and implant. At all times, care should be taken to assess and properly
rotate the components. If the knee is balanced and instability remains in flexion only, the
distal femur can be cut to elevate the joint line and allow for the insertion of a larger
polyethylene component. Approximately 50% of patients undergoing revision for the
management instability may require some amount of joint line elevation.5 Prior to
elevation of the joint line, posterior capsule release may be considered to allow for full
extension with a thicker polyethylene component.
Late instability in a previously well-functioning cruciate-retaining knee because of
suspected PCL incompetence can be managed via revision to an anterior lipped
polyethylene liner (if one exists for the index prosthesis) or to a posterior-stabilized
prosthesis. A constrained prosthesis should be considered during revision surgery if the
collateral ligaments are attenuated and proper mediolateral balancing cannot be
achieved via soft-tissue releases. Gradual attenuation of the PCL may lead to chronic
strain on the medial collateral ligament, resulting in mediolateral instability. A hinged
prosthesis should be considered if severe femoral bone loss involving the epicondyles
compromises collateral stability.
Mid-Flexion Instability
Definition and Causes
Instability in one or more planes between 30° and 90° of flexion
Joint line elevation and femoral malrotation are believed to play important roles.

Definition and Causes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
17/22

Although occasionally used interchangeably, mid-flexion instability and flexion instability
are different entities.6 The concept mid-flexion instability was introduced in 1990 after a
cadaver study found that joint line elevation caused instability at many angles
throughout ROM. In clinical practice, mid-flexion instability is used to describe any
instability (mediolateral, anterior-posterior, or rotational) between 30° and 90° of flexion.
Some surgeons question the existence of this type of instability and believe that it
merely represents general instability, except for stability in full extension because of
tight posterior capsular structures.
Although interest in mid-flexion instability recently has increased, this entity remains
controversial and generally is poorly understood. In TKA, balancing is performed at 0°
and 90°, neglecting angles in between. This practice achieves adequate balancing
throughout the entire ROM in some patients; however, in other patients it does not
because of patient-related, implant-related, and technique-related factors. Several
related factors have been proposed, including preoperative laxity, preoperative activity
level, joint line height, malrotation within the angles of instability, type of alignment,
restoration of the posterior offset, design of the femoral component (related to the
magnitude of the radius of curvature), and possible attenuation of collateral ligaments at
mid-range.
Findings

Findings
The symptoms of mid-flexion instability are not well described in the literature; however,
they may resemble those observed in patients with flexion instability but may be more
subtle. Symptoms of mid-flexion instability include mild instability and pain without the
knee giving way when rising from a sitting position or ascending or descending stairs.
Patients may report that they do not feel confident in their knee and may state general
dissatisfaction and limited function. Mid-flexion instability is assessed between 30° and
90° of flexion by performing mediolateral and anterior-posterior stress testing and by
evaluating rotation stability. Similar to flexion instability, recurrent effusions and diffuse
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
18/22

tenderness over ligamentous insertion points (mainly the pes anserinus and hamstring)
also may be present.
Management
Complete component revision usually is required.

Management
Poor understanding of the underlying cause of mid-flexion instability limits
management. In general, complete revision is necessary if objective findings, such as
restoration of the joint line, posterior offset, or a malrotated femoral component, can be
corrected. Additional data are necessary to guide the management of this difficult
pattern of instability.
Outcomes
Results of the management of instability are not as predictable as those of the management of
loosening or periprosthetic joint infection.
Revision of femoral and tibial components is necessary in most patients.

Outcomes
A paucity of literature exists on the nonsurgical management of instability, and
additional research is necessary to determine the effectiveness of quadriceps-
strengthening programs and bracing on the objective and subjective symptoms of
instability.
Simply exchanging the tibial polyethylene component may be tempting in patients with
flexion instability; however, this does not correct the gap mismatch because it adds
symmetrically to flexion and extension, possibly leading to inadequate extension.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:29 PM
AAOS | Instability After Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000511
19/22

Isolated polyethylene exchange may result in a 50% failure rate within 3 years; therefore,
this treatment option must be carefully considered before being offered as a solution to
the patient.7
Compared with revision surgery for the management of other aseptic loosening, revision
for the management of instability is not as predictable and is less successful with regard
to overall function and patient satisfaction. Patients should be informed that
expectations are not met with regard to pain relief, daily activity, and recreational
activities in 40% to 60% of patients undergoing revision.8 The literature indicates that
more predictable outcomes can be expected with revision of the femoral and tibial
components and with the use of femoral augments;9 however, much information about
this complication after TKA remains unknown. A shared decision-making process
between the surgeon and the patient is key to avoiding unreasonable expectations after
revision surgery for the management of instability.
Mark as Complete
